sections.heading: What does GORD feel like?
sections.body:
The NHS describes heartburn as a burning feeling in the middle of the chest, often with a sour taste, caused by stomach acid travelling up towards the throat. It is often worse after eating, when lying down and when bending over. If it keeps happening, it may be called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD.

NHS inform lists other possible symptoms, including bloating, belching, vomiting, a hoarse voice and a sore throat. NIDDK, a United States institute, describes GERD (the American spelling) as a more severe and longer-lasting condition in which reflux of stomach contents into the oesophagus, the food pipe, causes repeated symptoms or complications.

The NHS says common triggers include coffee, tomatoes, alcohol, chocolate, and fatty or spicy foods. Smoking, being overweight, pregnancy, stress and some painkillers such as ibuprofen are also listed.

sections.heading: Is reflux different in babies and children?
sections.body:
NICE guidance on reflux in children and young people describes regurgitation, when a baby brings milk back up, as common and normal in infancy. The NHS says a baby with reflux does not usually need to see a doctor if they are happy, healthy and gaining weight, and that babies usually grow out of it by the age of 1. It suggests a GP visit if a baby is not improving after trying ways to ease reflux, or if reflux is still happening after the age of 1.

For formula-fed babies who often regurgitate and are very distressed, NICE sets out steps for clinicians. These include reviewing the feeding history, trying smaller, more frequent feeds, and then trying a thickened formula.

A children's hospital leaflet lists coughing, gagging, trouble swallowing and wheezing among the symptoms to raise with a GP or health visitor.

sections.heading: How is GORD diagnosed, and are tests needed?
sections.body:
NHS inform says a GP can often diagnose GORD from the symptoms and may start treatment without any tests. NIDDK likewise says doctors usually diagnose it from symptoms and medical history. Testing is generally kept for people whose symptoms do not improve with lifestyle changes and medicines, or where a complication or another condition is suspected.

The NHS says tests such as a gastroscopy may be used for severe or persistent cases. A gastroscopy is an examination in which a thin tube with a camera is passed down the throat to look at the lining of the food pipe and stomach.

NHS inform advises seeing a GP if symptoms happen several times a week, if over-the-counter medicines are not helping, or if there are signs of something more serious such as persistent vomiting, vomiting blood or unexplained weight loss. The NHS notes that severe chest pain can occur and may be mistaken for a heart attack, and says urgent medical help is needed rather than a routine appointment. In an emergency, call 999.

sections.heading: What treatments are used for GORD?
sections.body:
The NHS says pharmacies sell antacids, which neutralise stomach acid, and alginates, which form a coating that protects the oesophagus from acid. These ease symptoms but will not cure the problem, and should not be taken regularly for long periods.

If lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines do not help, a GP may prescribe a proton pump inhibitor. This is a medicine, such as omeprazole or lansoprazole, that reduces how much acid the stomach makes. The NHS says some people need to take it on a long-term basis. If it does not control symptoms, a medicine known as an H2 receptor antagonist may be recommended.

The NHS says surgery is rarely needed. NHS inform describes it as an option if medication does not control symptoms.

sections.heading: Living with reflux: what self-care helps?
sections.body:
The NHS lists several self-care measures. These include eating smaller, more frequent meals, avoiding trigger foods, and not eating within three to four hours of bed. It also suggests avoiding tight waistbands, not smoking, cutting back on alcohol and losing weight if needed. Raising the head of the bed may also help, but the NHS says extra pillows are not recommended.

NIDDK says that for people who are overweight or have obesity, a doctor may suggest losing weight. It lists foods and drinks commonly linked to symptoms, including citrus fruits, tomatoes, chocolate, mint, caffeine, alcohol, high-fat foods and spicy foods. It adds that people react differently, so a doctor may suggest cutting out particular foods to see what helps.

sections.heading: What problems can reflux cause?
sections.body:
NHS inform says long-term damage to the oesophagus from leaking stomach acid can lead to ulcers, scarring and changes to the cells of the oesophagus, which can increase the risk of oesophageal cancer. A hospital leaflet says narrowings of the oesophagus, called strictures, are most commonly caused by scarring from acid reflux and usually cause difficulty swallowing that develops gradually.

Barrett's oesophagus is a change in the lining at the lower end of the oesophagus, usually found through endoscopy. Hospital leaflets say long-term acid reflux is thought to be the main driver, and the changed cells are not cancerous but carry a small increased risk of becoming so. NICE guidance says a history of reflux symptoms and obesity are the main risk factors.

NHS inform says a hiatus hernia, where part of the stomach pushes up through the diaphragm, makes reflux more likely.

faqs.q: Is acid reflux the same as heartburn?
faqs.a: The NHS describes heartburn as the burning feeling in the chest from acid travelling up towards the throat. If it keeps happening, it may be called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD. So heartburn is the symptom, and GORD is the longer-lasting condition behind it.

The NHS says antacids and alginates ease symptoms but will not cure the problem, and should not be taken regularly for long periods. A pharmacist can advise on them. If lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines are not helping, the NHS advises seeing a GP, who may prescribe a proton pump inhibitor, a medicine that reduces how much acid the stomach makes.

faqs.q: Is a camera test always needed for reflux?
faqs.a: No. NHS inform says a GP can often diagnose GORD from symptoms and may start treatment without tests. The NHS says tests such as a gastroscopy, where a thin tube with a camera is passed down the throat, may be used for severe or persistent cases.

faqs.q: Do babies grow out of reflux?
faqs.a: The NHS says babies usually grow out of reflux by the age of 1. It says a baby with reflux does not usually need to see a doctor if they are happy, healthy and gaining weight. It suggests a GP visit if the baby is not improving after trying ways to ease reflux, or if reflux is still happening after the age of 1.

faqs.q: When should someone see a doctor about heartburn?
faqs.a: The NHS advises seeing a GP if lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines are not helping, if heartburn happens most days, or if there are other symptoms such as food getting stuck in the throat, frequent sickness or weight loss for no reason. Severe chest pain needs urgent medical help rather than a routine appointment; in an emergency, call 999.

keyFacts.value: Acid reflux, GORD, GERD, heartburn (when the burning chest feeling is the main symptom)

keyFacts.value: Burning in the chest, sour taste in the mouth, sometimes hoarse voice or bloating

keyFacts.value: Smaller, more frequent meals; not eating just before bed; not smoking; pharmacist advice

keyFacts.value: Antacids and alginates ease symptoms but do not cure

sections.heading: What does osteoarthritis feel like, and does it get worse?
sections.body:
Pain and stiffness in the affected joints are the main features of osteoarthritis. NHS sources say the symptoms may come and go in episodes, which can be related to activity levels and even the weather. Pain is often worse with activity, and stiffness is typically worst after rest or in the morning, easing once a person starts to move. Versus Arthritis says a short spell of stiffness after rest is common.

The knees, hips and small joints of the hands are the most common areas affected, and the big toes and feet can also be involved.

The NHS says the condition does not necessarily get any worse over time. Symptoms vary from person to person and between different joints, and in more severe cases they can be continuous. Some people have osteoarthritis without many symptoms at all.

sections.heading: How is osteoarthritis diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP or other healthcare professional asks about the symptoms and examines the joints. NHS inform says there is no single definitive test for osteoarthritis. A NICE draft evidence review says that, without features pointing to another problem, osteoarthritis can be diagnosed through history and examination alone.

NHS inform says an X-ray is not currently recommended for diagnosing osteoarthritis, although one can show how much joint damage there is. For the hip and knee, an X-ray is sometimes used to help the diagnosis. Versus Arthritis says doctors rarely use an X-ray or blood test for knee problems, mainly to rule out other causes. MedlinePlus notes that X-rays may show loss of joint space and bone spurs, and that some people who have these changes have no symptoms.

MedlinePlus says blood tests do not help diagnose osteoarthritis, but they can check for other conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or gout. NHS inform lists joint pain, tenderness, stiffness, swelling and restricted movement as reasons to contact a GP practice.

sections.heading: What treatments are used for osteoarthritis?
sections.body:
The NHS says osteoarthritis cannot be cured but that a number of treatments can relieve the symptoms. It groups the main options into lifestyle measures, pain medication and supportive therapies. NICE guidance calls therapeutic exercise and weight management core treatments, and NHS inform describes keeping the joint active and strengthening the muscles around it as the best way to manage symptoms.

For pain, the NHS describes creams containing an anti-inflammatory medicine (topical NSAIDs) as often used for the knees and hands, and NICE advises offering one for knee osteoarthritis. Capsaicin cream is another option, and burning is its most common side effect. The NHS describes paracetamol as suitable for short-term use. NSAID tablets are generally considered if creams do not help, and because they can wear down the stomach lining, a medicine that reduces stomach acid may be given alongside them. Opioids such as codeine are generally limited to short-term use because of their side effects.

Steroid injections are sometimes offered when other treatments have not worked, and the NHS says they can ease pain for several weeks or months. NICE says to consider a corticosteroid injection into the joint when other medicines are ineffective or unsuitable.

sections.heading: What can help with osteoarthritis day to day?
sections.body:
The NHS says supportive aids such as shock-absorbing footwear, insoles, braces and walking sticks can reduce strain on the joints during everyday activities. Patient leaflets from NHS services describe pacing, which means balancing rest and activity, and note that taking on too much on a low-pain day can lead to worse pain afterwards. Supportive shoes are described as improving comfort and balance, and a walking stick can take pressure off an affected hip.

The leaflets describe heat as often suggested for stiffness or aching and cold for a sudden flare-up or swelling, with packs wrapped in a cloth. A physiotherapist can help build a plan guided by a person's symptoms, physical function and goals.

The NHS says GPs no longer prescribe glucosamine and chondroitin supplements on the NHS, because there is no strong evidence that they work.

sections.heading: When is surgery considered?
sections.body:
NHS inform says surgery is reserved for cases where other treatments have not been effective or where a joint is severely affected. It may greatly improve symptoms, but it cannot be guaranteed to resolve them fully. Versus Arthritis describes lifestyle changes, medication, therapies and, rarely, surgery as the ways to help.

MedlinePlus says non-surgical treatments often delay surgery or keep symptoms mild enough that it is not needed. The operations it lists include trimming damaged cartilage through a keyhole procedure (arthroscopy), realigning bone (osteotomy), fusing a joint, and partial or total joint replacement. NHS inform says joint replacement is the most common surgical option and that the decision is made with an orthopaedic surgeon, a doctor who specialises in bone and joint surgery.

faqs.a: The NHS says there is no cure for osteoarthritis, but treatments can relieve the symptoms. It groups the main options into lifestyle measures, pain medication and supportive therapies. The NHS also says the condition does not necessarily get any worse over time, and symptoms vary from person to person. NICE guidance describes therapeutic exercise and weight management as core treatments.

faqs.q: Is an X-ray needed to diagnose osteoarthritis?
faqs.a: NHS inform says an X-ray is not currently recommended for diagnosing osteoarthritis, although one can show how much joint damage is present. A GP asks about the symptoms and examines the joints, and there is no single definitive test. MedlinePlus notes that some people who have X-ray changes have no symptoms. Blood tests are used to look for other conditions, not to confirm osteoarthritis.

faqs.q: Do osteoarthritis symptoms come and go?
faqs.a: NHS sources say the symptoms may come and go in episodes, which can be related to activity levels and even the weather. Pain is often worse with activity, and stiffness is typically worst after rest or in the morning, easing with movement. Severity varies between people and between joints, and some people have osteoarthritis without many symptoms.

faqs.q: Do glucosamine and chondroitin supplements help?
faqs.a: The NHS says GPs no longer prescribe glucosamine and chondroitin on the NHS, because there is no strong evidence that they work. The options the NHS does describe are lifestyle measures, pain medication such as creams, and supportive therapies and aids such as footwear, insoles, braces and walking sticks.

faqs.q: Does everyone with osteoarthritis need surgery?
faqs.a: No. NHS inform says surgery is reserved for cases where other treatments have not been effective or where a joint is severely affected. MedlinePlus says non-surgical treatments often delay surgery or keep symptoms mild enough that it is not needed. When surgery is considered, the options include fusing a joint and partial or total joint replacement, decided with an orthopaedic surgeon.
